Ch 2: Hydrostatic Forces & Buoyancy

Lecture 2.3 · Text Ch 2.5–2.8 · Week of May 11th

2.3 — Buoyancy & Floating Bodies

Lecture 2.2 ended on a quiet promise. When we computed the vertical force on a curved surface, we found that if fluid sits above the surface the vertical force is the real weight of that column pointing down, but if the fluid is below the surface we imagine the column that would sit there and the force points up. A submerged body has fluid pressing up on its underside and down on its top — so it is nothing more than two curved surfaces stacked together, and the leftover upward force is exactly what we call buoyancy. This lecture turns that observation into a single, very usable result.

Archimedes’ principle

In the third century B.C., Archimedes worked out the whole idea without a single equation. Two statements capture it:

Archimedes’ Law of Buoyancy

1. Immersed body: a body immersed in a fluid feels a vertical buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces.

2. Floating body: a floating body displaces its own weight of the fluid in which it floats.

The force is always directed upward (against gravity) and depends only on the fluid and the displaced volume — not on the body’s material, shape detail, or depth.

The picture below is the classic demonstration. A 5 kg weight hung in air reads 5 kg on the scale; lowered into water it reads only 2 kg. The “missing” 3 kg of apparent weight is the buoyant force, and it is exactly the weight of the water that spilled into the small dish — the water the object pushed out of the way.

Archimedes’ law in a picture: the loss of apparent weight (5 kg → 2 kg) equals the weight of the displaced water collected in the side dish.

Why there is an upward force: two derivations

Both derivations look at the same submerged body and arrive at the same formula. They are worth seeing together because each one matches a tool we already have.

Two equivalent ways to add up the buoyant force. (a) Vertical force on the lower surface minus that on the upper surface. (b) Integrate the pressure difference over horizontal elemental columns through the body.
Approach (a) — forces on the upper and lower surfaces

Split the body into an upper surface (1) and a lower surface (2), exactly as in 2.2. The fluid pushes down on the top with force \(F_V(1)\) = weight of the fluid column above surface 1, and pushes up on the bottom with force \(F_V(2)\) = weight of the (imaginary) fluid column above surface 2. The net upward force is the difference:

\[ F_B = F_V(2) - F_V(1) = (\text{fluid weight above 2}) - (\text{fluid weight above 1}) \]

The two columns share the same top region and differ only by the slice of fluid that the body itself occupies. So the difference is simply the weight of fluid equal in volume to the body.

Approach (b) — summation of elemental pressure forces

Slice the body into thin vertical columns of horizontal area \(dA_H\). On each column the bottom pressure \(p_2\) exceeds the top pressure \(p_1\) (it is deeper), giving a net upward push \((p_2-p_1)\,dA_H\). Since \(p_2-p_1 = -\gamma\,(z_2 - z_1)\) for a fluid at rest, integrating over the body gives:

\[ F_B = \int_{\text{body}} (p_2 - p_1)\,dA_H = -\gamma \int (z_2 - z_1)\,dA_H = \gamma\,(\text{body volume}) \]

The integral \(\int (z_1 - z_2)\,dA_H\) is just the volume of the body, so the result is the same as approach (a): the buoyant force equals the specific weight of the fluid times the displaced volume.

Buoyant Force (Archimedes)

\[ F_B = \gamma_{\text{fluid}}\,\forall_{\text{displaced}} \]

\(F_B\) — buoyant force, directed vertically up (N) \(\gamma_{\text{fluid}}\) — specific weight of the fluid, \(\gamma=\rho g\) (N/m\(^3\)) \(\forall_{\text{displaced}}\) — volume of fluid displaced (m\(^3\))

When to use: any body fully or partly submerged in a fluid at rest — to find lift, apparent weight, cable tension, or the float/sink outcome. For a fully submerged body \(\forall_{\text{displaced}}\) is the whole body volume; for a floating body it is only the submerged portion.

When NOT to use: a body resting flat on the bottom with no fluid underneath it (no upward pressure face, so no buoyancy), or in accelerating/moving fluids. Always use displaced volume — never the above-water volume of a floating body.

Where the force acts: the centre of buoyancy

Pressure acts over the whole wetted surface, but the resultant buoyant force can be replaced by a single upward force through one point. That point is the centroid of the displaced volume — the centre of buoyancy \(B\). It is generally not the same point as the body’s centre of gravity \(CG\) (the centroid of the body’s mass). Their relative positions are what decide whether a floating body is stable, the topic that follows buoyancy in the course.

A floating body in vertical equilibrium. The weight \(W\) acts down through the centre of gravity \(CG\); the buoyant force \(F_B\) acts up through the centre of buoyancy \(B\) (centroid of the displaced volume). Displaced air above the waterline is negligible.
Centre of Buoyancy

The buoyant force passes through the centre of volume of the displaced fluid, called the centre of buoyancy \(B\). In vertical equilibrium a floating body settles until the buoyant force exactly balances its weight:

\[ F_B = \gamma_{\text{fluid}}\,\forall_{\text{displaced}} = W \quad(\text{floating body in equilibrium}) \]

Floating bodies

For a body that floats freely — nothing tethering or pushing it — the only two vertical forces are its weight and the buoyant force, so they must be equal. Setting \(F_B = W\) lets us solve for how deeply the body sits (its draft or submerged depth).

Floating Body — Displaces Its Own Weight

\[ F_B = W \;\Rightarrow\; \gamma_{\text{fluid}}\,\forall_{\text{sub}} = \gamma_{\text{body}}\,\forall_{\text{body}} \]

\(\forall_{\text{sub}}\) — submerged (displaced) volume (m\(^3\)) \(\forall_{\text{body}}\) — total volume of the body (m\(^3\)) \(\gamma_{\text{fluid}}\) — specific weight of fluid (N/m\(^3\)) \(\gamma_{\text{body}}\) — average specific weight of body (N/m\(^3\))

When to use: an object floating at rest with no external support — to find the waterline, submerged depth, or how high it rides. The weight side may be written as \(\gamma_{\text{body}}\forall_{\text{body}}\) or simply as the given weight \(W\).

When NOT to use: fully submerged tethered or supported bodies, where \(F_B \neq W\) because an extra force (cable, hand, bottom) closes the balance — there, put \(F_B\) into a full \(\sum F_V = 0\) instead.

Submerged Fraction of a Floating Body

\[ \frac{\forall_{\text{sub}}}{\forall_{\text{body}}} = \frac{\rho_{\text{body}}}{\rho_{\text{fluid}}} = \frac{SG_{\text{body}}}{SG_{\text{fluid}}} \]

\(\rho_{\text{body}}\) — density of the body (kg/m\(^3\)) \(\rho_{\text{fluid}}\) — density of the fluid (kg/m\(^3\)) \(SG\) — specific gravity, \(\rho/\rho_{\text{water}}\) (recall 1.2)

When to use: a quick read on what fraction of a floating object lies below the surface, or to compare densities. Follows directly from \(F_B=W\) once the \(g\) in \(\gamma=\rho g\) cancels. Example: ice (\(SG\approx0.92\)) floats in water with about 92% submerged.

When NOT to use: fully submerged bodies (fraction is 1 by definition) or layered fluids. If \(SG_{\text{body}} \ge SG_{\text{fluid}}\) the object does not float — it sinks.

★ Float, sink, or hover?

Imagine the body fully submerged and compare the largest possible buoyant force with the weight:

\(F_B > W\) (equivalently \(\rho_{\text{body}} < \rho_{\text{fluid}}\)) → net upward force, the body rises and floats, settling until the submerged part again gives \(F_B = W\).

\(F_B < W\) (\(\rho_{\text{body}} > \rho_{\text{fluid}}\)) → weight wins even when fully submerged, the body sinks.

\(F_B = W\) (\(\rho_{\text{body}} = \rho_{\text{fluid}}\)) → neutral buoyancy: the body hovers at any depth (how a submarine trims itself).

How to solve buoyancy problems

★ A reliable recipe

1. Draw a free-body diagram of the body. Mark the weight \(W\) down through the \(CG\), the buoyant force \(F_B\) up through \(B\), and any other vertical force — a cable tension \(T\), an applied push, or a support reaction.

2. Get \(\forall_{\text{displaced}}\): the full body volume if fully submerged, or the submerged portion if floating, then \(F_B = \gamma_{\text{fluid}}\forall_{\text{displaced}}\).

3. Apply vertical equilibrium \(\sum F_V = 0\) and solve for the unknown. The quantity \(W - F_B\) is the body’s apparent weight (what a scale or cable would read).

Watch the cable direction: a tether to the floor holds a buoyant body down (tension acts downward on the body); a cable from above holds a heavy body up (tension acts upward). The sign in \(\sum F_V = 0\) follows the picture.

Worked examples

Example 1 — Tension in a tethered instrument package

An instrument package weighing \(W = 258\text{ N}\) is held by a cable to the seabed and is completely immersed in seawater (\(\gamma_{sw} = 10.05\text{ kN/m}^3\)). The package is a rectangular box \(0.6\text{ m} \times 0.3\text{ m} \times 0.45\text{ m}\). Find the tension in the cable.

Example 1 setup. The buoyant package is anchored to the sea bottom by a cable; the box is fully submerged.
▸ Show full solution

Thought process

The box is fully submerged, so the displaced volume is the entire box volume. It is anchored to the floor, which is the clue that the package is buoyant — if it weren’t, the cable would go slack. So \(F_B > W\), the net of weight and buoyancy is upward, and the cable pulls the box down to hold it in place.

FBD (vertical only): buoyant force \(F_B\) up, weight \(W\) down, cable tension \(T\) down. Then \(\sum F_V = 0\) gives \(T\).

Given: \(W = 258\text{ N}\); box \(0.6\times0.3\times0.45\text{ m}\), fully immersed; \(\gamma_{sw} = 10.05\text{ kN/m}^3 = 10\,050\text{ N/m}^3\).

Find: cable tension \(T\).

Displaced volume.

\[ \forall = (0.45\text{ m})(0.6\text{ m})(0.3\text{ m}) = 0.081\text{ m}^3 \]

Buoyant force.

\[ F_B = \gamma_{sw}\,\forall = (10\,050\text{ N/m}^3)(0.081\text{ m}^3) = 814\text{ N} \]

Vertical equilibrium. Taking up as positive, with \(T\) acting downward (cable to the floor):

\[ \sum F_V = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; F_B - W - T = 0 \]

\[ T = F_B - W = 814\text{ N} - 258\text{ N} = 556\text{ N} \]

Answer

\(T = 556\text{ N}\). The cable is in tension, holding the buoyant package down against an \(814\text{ N}\) upward buoyant force.

Used: Buoyant Force (#38) inside a vertical force balance \(\sum F_V = 0\).

Example 2 — Will a steel pipe float or sink in glycerin?

A steel pipe has an outside diameter of \(168\text{ mm}\). A \(1\text{ m}\) length of the pipe weighs \(277\text{ N}\). Would the pipe float or sink in glycerin (\(SG = 1.26\))?

Example 2 setup. A 1 m length of steel pipe in glycerin.
▸ Show full solution

Thought process

To decide float vs sink, assume the pipe is fully submerged and compute the largest possible buoyant force. If that maximum still cannot match the weight, the pipe sinks. The displaced volume of a fully submerged length is the outer cylinder volume \(\frac{\pi}{4}D^2 L\) (based on the outside diameter).

The glycerin’s specific weight is \(\gamma = SG\cdot\gamma_{\text{water}} = 1.26\,(9.81\text{ kN/m}^3)\).

Given: \(D = 0.168\text{ m}\), \(L = 1\text{ m}\), \(W = 277\text{ N}\), glycerin \(SG = 1.26\), \(\gamma_{\text{water}} = 9.81\text{ kN/m}^3\).

Find: does the pipe float or sink?

Maximum buoyant force (fully submerged).

\[ F_B = \gamma_{\text{glyc}}\,\forall = SG\,\gamma_{\text{water}}\left(\frac{\pi}{4}D^2 L\right) \]

\[ F_B = (1.26)(9.81\text{ kN/m}^3)\left(\frac{\pi\,(0.168\text{ m})^2}{4}\right)(1\text{ m}) \]

\[ F_B = 0.274\text{ kN} = 274\text{ N} \]

Compare with the weight.

\[ F_B = 274\text{ N} \;<\; W = 277\text{ N} \]

Even fully submerged, the buoyant force cannot support the pipe’s weight, so the pipe goes to the bottom.

Answer

The pipe sinks — its maximum buoyant force \(274\text{ N}\) is just short of its \(277\text{ N}\) weight (a margin of only \(3\text{ N}\)).

Used: Buoyant Force (#38) with specific gravity \(\gamma = SG\,\gamma_{\text{water}}\) (recall 1.2), compared against the weight.

Example 3 — Floating wooden cone

A solid wooden cone floats in water. The cone is \(30\text{ cm}\) high, its vertex angle is \(90^\circ\), and it floats with the vertex pointing down. (a) Derive a general equation for the depth the cone goes under water. (b) How much of the cone protrudes above the water if the specific gravity of the wood is \(0.729\)?

Example 3 setup. The cone floats vertex-down; only a similar smaller cone of height \(h\) is submerged.
▸ Show full solution

Thought process

The cone floats freely, so \(F_B = W\). The submerged part is a smaller cone (vertex-down) of height \(h\) and base radius \(r\); the whole cone has height \(H\) and base radius \(R\). The two cones are similar, so \(r/h = R/H\). Writing both the buoyant force and the weight as a specific weight times a cone volume, the radii and the constant \(\frac{\pi}{3}\) cancel and leave a clean ratio in the heights.

Given: total height \(H = 30\text{ cm}\), floats vertex-down, \(SG_{\text{wood}} = 0.729\), fluid is water.

Find: (a) general expression for submerged depth \(h\); (b) protrusion \(H - h\).

Geometry for the derivation (schematic, not to scale). Full cone: height \(H\), base radius \(R\). Submerged cone: height \(h\), radius \(r\). Similar triangles give \(r/h = R/H\).

Set up \(F_B = W\). A cone of base radius \(a\) and height \(b\) has volume \(\frac{\pi}{3}a^2 b\). The buoyant force is the weight of the displaced water (the submerged cone); the weight is the wood’s specific weight times the full cone volume:

\[ F_B = \gamma_{\text{water}}\,\frac{\pi}{3} r^2 h, \qquad W = \gamma_{\text{wood}}\,\frac{\pi}{3} R^2 H = SG\,\gamma_{\text{water}}\,\frac{\pi}{3} R^2 H \]

Setting \(F_B = W\) and cancelling \(\gamma_{\text{water}}\frac{\pi}{3}\):

\[ r^2 h = SG\,R^2 H \]

Use similar triangles \(r/h = R/H\), i.e. \(r = R\,(h/H)\), so \(r^2 = R^2 h^2 / H^2\):

\[ \frac{R^2 h^2}{H^2}\,h = SG\,R^2 H \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{h^3}{H^2} = SG\,H \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{h^3}{H^3} = SG \]

\[ \boxed{\,h = H\,(SG)^{1/3}\,} \qquad\text{(a)} \]

(b) Numbers. With \(SG = 0.729\) and \((0.729)^{1/3} = 0.9\):

\[ h = (30\text{ cm})(0.729)^{1/3} = (30\text{ cm})(0.9) = 27\text{ cm} \]

\[ H - h = 30\text{ cm} - 27\text{ cm} = 3\text{ cm} \]

Answer

(a) \(h = H\,(SG)^{1/3}\).   (b) the cone is submerged \(27\text{ cm}\), so \(3\text{ cm}\) protrudes above the water.

Used: Floating-body balance \(F_B = W\) (#39) with the buoyant force (#38), cone volume \(\frac{\pi}{3}r^2h\), and similar triangles \(r/h = R/H\).

★ Lecture recap

One formula does most of the work: \(F_B = \gamma_{\text{fluid}}\,\forall_{\text{displaced}}\), always upward, acting through the centre of buoyancy \(B\).

Fully submerged → displaced volume is the whole body; put \(F_B\) into \(\sum F_V = 0\) together with any cable or support. Floating freely → \(F_B = W\), and the submerged fraction equals \(SG_{\text{body}}/SG_{\text{fluid}}\).

Float / sink / hover is decided by comparing densities: lighter than the fluid floats, denser sinks, equal hovers.
